To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the axial channel of upper Monterey Canyon is a dynamic, erosional environment that has undergone major morphological changes during a six-month interval; (2) the channel floor is dominated by sand waves that are strongly asymmetric, indicating net downcanyon sediment transport; (3) the canyon head is a depositional area where sediment is transported from the canyon head to the nearshore environment; and (4) the net volume of sediment transported through the canyon head during a six-month period
the upper Monterey Canyon is a dynamic system that is actively reshaping itself.
(1) sediment transport in Monterey Canyon is episodic and (2) sediment transport is strongly influenced by seasonal variations in the strength and direction of nearshore currents.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the short-term (hours to months) evolution of the upper 4-km of Monterey Canyon and its adjacent shelf.
the geomorphologic evolution of the upper Monterey Canyon, including the processes that control the formation of its terraces, sand waves, gullies, and other features.
the processes of sediment erosion, transport and deposition in the upper 3 km of Monterey Canyon.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the upper part of Monterey Canyon is a dynamic system in which erosion and deposition are occurring at a rate of 5.3 m/yr (±2.5 m/yr).
erosion of the canyon floor is balanced by sediment deposition on the canyon rim, but the canyon rim is also eroding.
erosion and deposition in the upper 2 km of Monterey Canyon is highly episodic and occurs over a range of timescales, from minutes to months.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
sediment erosion and deposition in Monterey Canyon is episodic and highly localized.
sediment transport processes in Monterey Canyon are episodic and that the sediment budget is in a state of near balance.
the canyon is a net sediment sink, but that there are significant short-term variations in the rates and locations of erosion and deposition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
small-scale changes in canyon morphology are common and that the canyon is a dynamic system.
serial bathymetry can be a powerful tool for quantifying short-term erosion and deposition in the nearshore environment.
the upper Monterey Canyon is a dynamic system that is undergoing continuous change, and the canyon head is an active site of sediment transport, erosion, and deposition.
